newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition reaches post monopoly compromise.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition reaches post monopoly compromise.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition on Tuesday agreed to extend the monopoly of national post office Deutsche Post AG for five years to the end of 2002, but only for letters weighing under 100 grams (3.5 ounces).
The decision was a compromise between Kohl's conservatives and their free-market Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners.

Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch of the Christian Social Union, sister party of Kohl's Christian Democrats, wanted the post office to keep its monopoly on items weighing up to 350 grams (12.4 ounces), while the FDP wanted the monopoly scrapped to let competitors into the market.

"We are not maintaining the monopoly because we are scared of competition, but because we want the company to be able to make the transition from a state-owned company to a private enterprise," Boetsch told a news conference.

But Deutsche Post said the compromise would have disastrous consequences for customers and workers and open up 6.7 billion marks ($3.9 billion) of its total 15.5 billion marks turnover to competition.
The decision still has to be approved by the cabinet and then go before parliament.
It came a day after 23,000 postal workers converged on Bonn to protest against plans for postal liberalisation. Last week there were stoppages at post offices in 52 cities.

Postal workers' union Deutsche Postgewerkschaft (DPG), which organised the march, said tens of thousands of jobs would be lost if the postal monopoly was completely removed in 1998, contributing to Germany's spiralling unemployment crisis.

"The government has a responsibility for the social well-being and employment of postal workers. The far-reaching liberalisation of the post office must not be allowed to lead to social decline," said DPG chairman Kurt van Haaren.
Van Haaren called on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who sharply criticised the compromise, to help block the plan in the upper house of parliament.
"The coalition's sloppy compromise will lead to job losses, and to lower quality and higher cost of services," SPD parliamentary post spokesman Hans Martin Bury said.
FDP free-market supporters called the decision a victory.

"With this (compromise) the timing of full liberalisation is set for January 1, 2003. Competitors of Deutsche Post have a clear timeframe to make the appropriate investment plans," said FDP negotiation leader Rainer Funke.

Deutsche Post said the company's massive annual pension burden of five billion marks could no longer be financed under the coalition's plan and said stamp prices would have to rise to cover these costs.

It also said the reforms could mean a large number of post offices would have to close and said the German market was being opened up to competition without Deutsche Post having the same opportunity to penetrate foreign markets.

The DPG union fears the new postal law will open the market up to "cherry-picking", in which rivals will be able to operate in the most lucrative markets, ignoring less attractive market segments, such as delivery to remote locations. ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
